name: Minot's Ledge
note: One flash, four, then three. Since 1 May 1894 the light has flashed this group, and because "I love you" has one, four and three letters, the tower is known locally as the "I love you" light. Count the dark between groups: it is what separates 1, 4 and 3 from a run of eight.

name: Cape Hatteras
note: A one-second flash and a six-and-a-half-second eclipse: 7.5 s in all. The flash count tells you nothing here, so the period has to: time two flashes, not one.

name: Portland Head
note: The same grammar as Hatteras, a single white flash, but nearly twice as fast. Side by side, the two lights differ only in their period.

name: Fastnet
place: Fastnet Rock, off County Cork, Ireland
note: Another single white flash, at five seconds. Three lights in a row with the same letters show why the number after them matters most.

name: Bishop Rock
note: Two flashes close together, then a long dark. A group is read as one word: the pair belongs together because the gap inside it is much shorter than the gap after it.

name: Eddystone
note: Two lights on one tower. The main light flashes white in pairs; a lower window shows a red isophase light toward the Hand Deeps, a hazard to the west-northwest. See the red and you are in the arc that covers the danger.

name: Cape Byron
place: Byron Bay, New South Wales, Australia
note: A slow white flash high on the headland, and a fixed red light seven metres below it with a far shorter charted range: 27 nautical miles for the white, 8 for the red.

name: Sandy Hook
note: A fixed light: no rhythm at all. A steady light says nothing distinctive about itself, which is why the IALA buoyage system does not use fixed lights on its marks.
